section_title: What does David ask of the army before the battle?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 Then David reviewed his troops and appointed over them commanders of thousands and of hundreds. 2 He sent out the troops, a third under Joab, a third under Joab’s brother Abishai son of Zeruiah, and a third under Ittai the Gittite. And the king said to the troops, “I will surely march out with you as well.” 3 But the people pleaded, “You must not go out! For if we have to flee, they will not care about us. Even if half of us die, they will not care. But you are worth ten thousand of us. It is better now if you support us from the city.” 4 “I will do whatever seems best to you,” the king replied. So he stood beside the gate, while all the troops marched out by hundreds and by thousands. 5 Now the king had commanded Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, “Treat the young man Absalom gently for my sake.” And all the people heard the king’s orders to each of the commanders regarding Absalom.

6 So David’s army marched into the field to engage Israel, and the battle took place in the forest of Ephraim. 7 There the people of Israel were defeated by David’s servants, and the slaughter was great that day—twenty thousand men. 8 The battle spread over the whole countryside, and that day the forest devoured more people than the sword.

context_lines: David organizes his forces under Joab, Abishai and Ittai, giving each command of a third. He offers to go with them, but they urge him to remain in the city because the enemy’s main target is the king. David accepts their advice.

As the troops leave, David publicly orders the commanders to treat Absalom gently for his sake. Everyone hears. The battle in the forest of Ephraim ends in a major defeat for Absalom’s forces, with twenty thousand men killed. The account says the forest devours more people than the sword, emphasizing the danger of the scattered fighting.
common_interpretation_lines: [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/2_samuel/18.htm) highlights the contrast between Absalom wanting David killed and David wanting Absalom spared. He sees mercy toward a son who has acted as an enemy.

[Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-samuel/) gives several possible reasons for David’s order, including affection, awareness of his own failures and a desire to leave time for repentance. He also includes a criticism of mercy that fails to confront a violent rebel. The tension between David’s concern as a father and his responsibility as king is real; interpreters do not all put the same emphasis on it.

The forest’s role is stated without a full explanation of how each death happens. Detailed accounts of hidden pits, wild animals or particular escape routes are possible reconstructions, not a description supplied by the narrator.
